reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A lobular panniculitis with vasculitis presenting as tender, indurated, often ulcerating nodules on the posterior lower legs (calves)
Predominantly affects women, and lesions tend to be more posterior than the anterior shins typical of erythema nodosum
Lesions frequently ulcerate and heal with atrophic scarring and pigmentation, distinguishing it from non-ulcerating erythema nodosum
When associated with tuberculosis it is regarded as a tuberculid, an immune (hypersensitivity) reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than direct skin infection
The term nodular vasculitis is used for clinically and histologically identical disease without demonstrable tuberculous association
A strongly positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay supports the tuberculid form
Cases linked to tuberculosis respond to antituberculous therapy, so evaluating for latent or active infection is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Erythema induratum is a lobular panniculitis accompanied by vasculitis of the small and medium vessels within the subcutaneous fat, leading to ischaemic fat necrosis, nodule formation, and ulceration. In the classic Bazin form it represents a tuberculid: a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial antigens disseminated from a distant focus, rather than viable organisms in the skin, so mycobacterial cultures of lesions are typically negative while molecular tests may detect mycobacterial DNA. Identical disease without tuberculous association is termed nodular vasculitis and may follow other infections, drugs, or chronic venous insufficiency.
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional or excisional skin biopsy capturing subcutaneous fat to show lobular panniculitis with vasculitis
Tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay
Chest radiograph and evaluation for active or latent tuberculosis
Tissue mycobacterial staining, culture, and polymerase chain reaction for mycobacterial DNA
Assessment of venous insufficiency in the lower limbs
Screening for alternative infective, drug, or systemic triggers in non-tuberculous cases
redFlags: Evidence of active tuberculosis requiring prompt antituberculous treatment and public-health measures
Chronic non-healing ulceration with secondary infection
Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) suggesting disseminated infection or systemic vasculitis
Recurrent disease despite treatment, prompting re-evaluation of the underlying cause
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing with recurrent crops of nodules and scarring; tuberculid cases usually improve substantially with antituberculous therapy, whereas idiopathic nodular vasculitis may persist and require anti-inflammatory treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing it with erythema nodosum and missing the posterior-leg distribution, ulceration, and vasculitis
Taking a biopsy too superficial to sample the subcutaneous fat
Failing to investigate for tuberculosis before attributing the disease to another cause
Overlooking treatable contributors such as chronic venous insufficiency or a drug trigger
